sections.h2: What shapes a Corpus Christi sale
sections.html:
Two things matter most: condition and timing. A well kept house can do well on the market, but one with storm damage, an estate attached or tenants inside often sells faster to a buyer who accepts it as it is.

Corpus Christi is a seaport on the west end of Corpus Christi Bay, the county seat of Nueces County and the largest city on the South Texas coast. It sits where Interstate 37 meets U.S. highways 77 and 181, 210 miles southwest of Houston. Salt air, wind and storm history make roofs, windows and foundations the first things coastal buyers check.

  • Open listing: widest reach for a house that shows well.
  • Owner sale: no commission, more paperwork for you.
  • Cash purchase: quicker and as-is, useful after storm damage or for an estate.

A hurricane on September 14, 1919 destroyed much of the North Beach area and the central business district, and the city has lived with coastal weather ever since. Buyers, insurers and lenders often ask about past damage. Keep repair receipts, permits for storm work and insurance claim records together, since they back up every answer you give.

Under city rules, renting any part or all of a residence for under 30 days, and for at least 12 hours, makes it a short-term rental, and every such property must be registered. Permits are valid for the calendar year and renewed each January. Hotel occupancy tax filing applies to short-term rentals, hotels and bed and breakfasts.

The ordinance approved on June 28, 2022 allows rentals with restrictions in single-family districts citywide, except in single-family districts within the Padre and Mustang Island area plan.

Permit typeWho is on siteLimit

The city paused new Type 1 permits while staff prepare changes for council, and permits valid through December 31, 2026 stay active. It also directed staff to apply the density limit to renewals, with at least one Type 2 rental per block face. Rules may have changed, so ask Development Services at (361) 826-3240 for the current version.

Applications ask for owner and agent contacts, a floor plan with sleeping areas, a guest maximum and exits, and a 24-hour contact person. Ask the city for the current fee. Do not tell a buyer a permit transfers with the house unless the city confirms it.

sections.h2: Where deeds and tax records live
sections.html:
City parcels in Nueces County are filed at the Nueces County clerk, and the appraisal district for that county sets values. Addresses near the city edge can lie in a neighboring county, so your latest tax bill is the quickest check.

To be accepted for filing, a deed must be acknowledged or have two witnesses. The clerk manual's price list puts page one at costs $5.00 and each later page $4.00, with surcharges for names past five and for records funds. The clerk can quote today's rates, and your title company normally does the filing itself.

sections.h2: What happens if property taxes go unpaid
sections.html:
Miss January 31 and the bill is delinquent on February 1. That day interest of one percent a month begins and a six percent penalty attaches, climbing to 12 percent by July 1. An attorney for the taxing unit may tack on up to 20 percent more.

Each year's tax lien forms on January 1 and travels with the house through any sale, which means a buyer cannot get clear title while back taxes remain. The title company settles the balance from your proceeds at closing. Seniors, disabled owners and owners with a disabled veteran exemption may use installments, and some collectors offer payment plans up to 36 months on a homestead.

sections.h2: A land contract or an occupant in the house
sections.html:
Under a contract for deed, sometimes called an installment land contract, title stays with the seller until the buyer has paid everything. Texas Property Code chapter 5, subchapter D governs those for residences, and the purchaser has a statutory right to cancel, so get legal advice before selling a house under such a contract.

When someone stays after being told to go, Property Code chapter 24B lets an owner ask the sheriff or constable to remove them, but only if conditions are met. One is that the occupant is not a relative or a current or former tenant. A removal done wrongly can bring a lawsuit. Failing that, the normal path is a justice court eviction suit.

sections.h2: What to gather before an offer
sections.html:
Pull together the deed, loan payoff, tax bill, insurance claim history and permits for any storm work. Coastal buyers raise flood and wind coverage early, so know what your policy covers and which company writes it.

Line up offers by net proceeds and by weeks to closing. A cash buyer may close sooner and will price in repairs, while a listing may net more after a longer wait. Have each buyer state in writing who pays title, recording and the tax split.

  • Does the buyer accept the house with storm damage unrepaired?
  • Can an open insurance claim be assigned, or must it be settled first?
  • How soon are funds available once the title company clears the file?

Anyone relocating or settling an estate may prize a firm closing date above a few extra dollars, so give certainty weight next to price.

Buyers on the coast look past paint and flooring to the envelope of the house. Expect questions about the age of the roof, whether windows are impact rated, how the foundation has held up and whether the house has ever flooded. Answer them with documents, not impressions.

If repairs are still undone, say so early. A buyer who learns about unrepaired damage at inspection will renegotiate, while one who knew from the start has already priced it in. A cash buyer will quote you for the house as it stands, which can save you from paying contractors before you sell.

Compare more than price. A buyer paying cash can often close in a few weeks, while one using a loan needs an appraisal and an inspection first. Put each offer's closing date, repair terms and title costs side by side, then pick the combination that fits your move.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works here
sections.html: The buyer looks at the house, usually once, and makes a written offer reflecting repairs. After you accept, the title company searches the records and orders payoffs, and you pick the closing date. With no lender, no appraisal can delay the schedule. Roof, window and foundation condition drive most of the discount on a coastal house.

faqs.q: Is Corpus Christi the county seat of Nueces County?
faqs.a: Yes. City parcels are recorded at the Nueces County clerk's office.

faqs.q: May I operate a short-term rental in Corpus Christi?
faqs.a: Only with a registration permit. The city requires one for any rental under 30 days, and the rules are under review, so ask Development Services which permit type applies and whether new ones are issued.

faqs.q: What happens to a rental permit when I sell?
faqs.a: Do not assume it carries over. Permits are issued annually and renewals face density rules, so get the city's answer before you describe the permit to a buyer.

faqs.q: When do property taxes go delinquent?
faqs.a: On February 1 for most bills. Penalty and interest begin that day, and the penalty grows each month through July 1.

faqs.q: Do I need to keep hurricane repair records?
faqs.a: Keep them. Buyers, insurers and lenders often ask about past damage, and receipts back up your answers.
